sermon:
There is a man I know who keeps every receipt. Not for taxes. For proof. He cannot rest until he can show, on paper, that he paid his way, that nothing was given to him he did not first deserve. He carries his ledger like a shield. And he is exhausted by it. He has never once felt rich, because in his accounting wealth is something you are always still earning.

Paul opens this letter to a man like that. To a whole church of them. And before he gives a single command, before he asks for anything, he writes one of the longest sentences in the New Testament — in the Greek it runs unbroken from verse three to verse fourteen — and the sentence is a tour of a vault that already belongs to people who own nothing.

**The blessing is already given**

"Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 1:3). Read it slowly. Has blessed. Past tense. Every blessing. Not most. Already in the heavenly places, not pending, not conditional on a better week. Paul is not promising what God might do. He is reporting what God has done.

And then he traces it through the three persons of the one God. The Father chose us before the foundation of the world — before there was a world to be good in, before any of us had a record to read. The Son redeemed us through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace. The Spirit sealed us, a deposit guaranteeing the inheritance until we acquire possession of it. Chosen, bought, sealed. There is nothing in that chain a man contributes. There is no place to slip your receipt in.

**For the praise of his glory**

Three times the passage circles back to the same refrain: to the praise of his glorious grace. To the praise of his glory. To the praise of his glory. This is the engine under everything. God did not save us mainly because we were drowning, though we were. He saved us for himself, that the wealth of his grace would be on display forever. That offends the man with the ledger, because it means he is not the point. And it frees the man with the ledger, because it means the security of his salvation does not rest on his performance but on God's purpose to be praised.

I have stood at hospital beds where this was the only thing left standing. A woman with weeks to live, who could no longer pray well, who could not remember her best moments, asking me whether God still wanted her. And the answer was not in anything she had done. It was that she was chosen before the foundation of the world, sealed by a Spirit she could not feel. Every spiritual blessing was already hers, in Christ, while she could do nothing but receive.

I confess I preach this more easily than I believe it. I keep a ledger too. I measure my standing by my output, by the week's faithfulness, and on bad weeks I quietly assume God's regard has dropped with my numbers. That is unbelief dressed as humility. Paul will not let it stand.

**The phrase that decides everything**

Everything in this passage hangs on two words repeated eleven times: in Christ. In him chosen. In him redeemed. In him sealed. The blessings are not handed to us across a distance to keep in our own account. They are located in a person, and we have them only because we are in him. This is why nothing can be earned and nothing can be lost. To lose the blessing you would have to be pried out of Christ, and the Father who gathered all things in heaven and on earth into one will not allow it.

So put down the ledger. Not because your record is clean. Because it has been answered, paid in blood, sealed by the Spirit, secured for the praise of his glory.

Nothing was left for you to earn.

A man can stand in a room he owns and feel like a trespasser. I have watched it happen to new believers. They have been told, truthfully, that they are forgiven, adopted, rich beyond counting — and they nod, and they go home, and they live like beggars. The deed is in their name. They cannot feel the house is theirs.

That is the problem Paul addresses next. He has just spent twelve verses describing the vault of blessing that already belongs to the church. Now he prays. And notice what he does not pray for. He does not ask God to give them more. He asks God to open their eyes to what they already have.

**A prayer for sight, not supply**

"That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened" (Ephesians 1:17-18). The eyes of your hearts. Not new resources, new perception. Paul is convinced their poverty is not in their account but in their sight.

And he names three things he wants them to see. The hope of his calling — that the God who called them has a future for them as certain as his own character. The riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints — and read that carefully, because it may mean God's inheritance in us, that we are the treasure he is gathering. And the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe. Three things owned, three things unseen, three things that change a person the moment they come into focus.

I think most of our spiritual exhaustion is not a supply problem. It is a sight problem. We pray for God to send what he has already given, and we do not see it arrive because it was here all along.

**The measure of the power**

When Paul reaches the third thing, the power, he cannot leave it abstract. He needs us to know how much power is at work toward us. So he reaches for the largest event he can name. The same power, he says, that God worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion.

That is the gauge. Not the strength you mustered last Tuesday. The strength that emptied a tomb. The power directed toward you, the believer, is resurrection power, the same exertion of God that pulled the dead Christ back through death and lifted him above every name that is named, in this age and the one to come. If you have ever wondered whether God has enough to get you home, the answer is the resurrection.

I need this as much as anyone listening. I can describe resurrection power in a sermon and then go home and pray as though God were running low. That is the unbelief Paul is fighting. He does not scold it. He prays against it.

**Seated, and therefore the head**

Then the prayer climbs to its summit. God "put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all." The risen Christ is not seated as a private victory. He is seated as head over all things, and given in that authority to the church. The body is joined to the head. What is true of him reaches down into us.

This is where the Christ connection becomes personal. You do not borrow his power from a distance. You are his body. The risen Lord is not a hero you admire across the centuries; he is the head to which you are joined, and the fullness that fills all in all is poured into the very people who feel emptiest.

So if you are living like a trespasser in a house you own, the answer is not to work harder for the deed. It is to ask God to turn on the light. Pray Paul's prayer over your own dim heart. Ask for eyes.

You already have what you cannot see.

No one resuscitates a corpse by encouraging it. You do not coach the dead. You do not give the dead a plan, a better attitude, a second chance to try harder. The dead need one thing, and it is not from inside them.

That is the word Paul chooses to describe what we were. Not sick. Not weakened. Not struggling. Dead. "And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked" (Ephesians 2:1). He says it twice in this paragraph, and everything hinges on whether we will believe him.

**The honest diagnosis**

We resist the word dead because we know we were busy. We were walking, Paul says — following the course of this world, the prince of the power of the air, the desires of the body and the mind. The dead in this passage are active. They are not lying still; they are running, achieving, sinning with energy. But they are running away from God, and a man can be vigorously, productively dead.

Then the verdict lands without cushion: "by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind." By nature. Not by accident, not by a few bad decisions that could be reversed with better information. This was our condition at the root, and it was shared. Paul does not exempt himself. We — all of us — were among them. I will not stand over this text and read it as someone else's diagnosis. It was mine. I was not a good man who needed polishing. I was a dead man who needed raising.

This is the floor the whole chapter is built on, and the floor has to be this low, because the grace that comes next has to be that high.

**But God**

The most important two words in the letter, maybe in the Bible, arrive here. "But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved." Even when we were dead. Not after we improved, not once we showed promise. While we were still corpses, God acted. The verb is his. He made us alive. We supplied the death; he supplied the life.

And he did not stop at the morgue. He raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly places. The believer is already, in Christ, where Christ is. The same seating Paul described for the risen Lord in chapter one is now described for us. We are seated with him. The future is so secure it is spoken in the past tense.

Why? "So that in the coming ages he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus." Again the purpose runs back to God's glory. We are exhibits of mercy, evidence for all the ages to come of what grace can do with the dead.

**No room to boast**

Then the most quoted lines, and the most flattened. "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast." Even the faith is not a contribution we managed; the whole thing is gift, end to end, precisely so that no one can stand at the last day with a receipt.

But Paul does not end on passivity. "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them." Saved by grace, not by works — and then saved for works God laid out in advance. The good life is the result, never the cause. Grace does not leave us on the table; it stands us up and points us down a road already prepared.

The Christ connection is the whole thing: made alive with Christ, raised with Christ, seated with Christ. Our resurrection is not a separate miracle we hope for. It is his, given to us.

Grace from first breath to last.

In the temple Paul knew, there was a wall. Not a metaphor. A stone barrier in the temple courts with an inscription warning Gentiles that to pass it was to forfeit their lives. The architecture itself announced who belonged and who did not. A man could see his exclusion in masonry.

Paul writes to people who lived on the wrong side of that wall, and he tells them to remember it. "Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh" were "separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world" (Ephesians 2:11-12). He wants them to feel the old distance before he tells them it is gone.

**Remember the distance**

This is a hard discipline, remembering what we were. We prefer to forget. But Paul knows that people who forget how far off they were will not marvel at being brought near, and will quietly rebuild walls of their own. So he piles up the words. Separated. Alienated. Strangers. No hope. Without God. Five descriptions of a single condition: outside, with no claim and no key.

And then the turn, in the same grammar as chapter two's first turn. "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ." The distance was real, and the means of crossing it was not a relaxed policy or a softened standard. It was blood. The wall did not fall because God decided it did not matter. It fell because Christ absorbed in his own body what the wall existed to mark.

**He himself is our peace**

"For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility." Notice Paul does not say Christ made peace, as if peace were a treaty he negotiated and then left us to keep. He himself is our peace. The peace is a person. The two hostile peoples are not reconciled by meeting in the middle; they are both reconciled to God in one body through the cross, and so to each other.

The result is something genuinely new. "That he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace." Not Jews who tolerate Gentiles. Not Gentiles who adopt Jewish custom. One new man. A third thing that did not exist before, made out of the two by killing the hostility in the cross.

I have to confess how slowly the church has believed this. We have built our own walls — of class, of color, of style, of which side of town a person comes from — inside the very body where the dividing wall was supposed to be rubble. I have pastored churches that prayed this text on Sunday and sorted themselves by it on Monday. The hostility Christ killed, we have quietly resurrected, and called it preference.

**Built into a dwelling**

Paul ends with a building, but not a wall this time. The two peoples are now "fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone." The whole structure is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord, "a dwelling place for God by the Spirit." The temple that once had a wall keeping Gentiles out is replaced by a temple made of the very people who were kept out, with God himself living inside it.

The Christ connection is the cornerstone. He is the stone that holds the new building square, and every wall we rebuild is a denial of the cornerstone we claim to be set on. If he is our peace, then a church that keeps people far off is preaching against its own foundation.

Two peoples, one body, no wall.

Paul begins a sentence and cannot finish it. "For this reason I, Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles" — and then he stops. He will not pick the thread up again for eleven verses. Something interrupts him, and the something is the sheer weight of what he has been given to announce. He gets to the word Gentiles and the wonder of it derails the grammar.

What could so interrupt a man? Paul calls it the mystery. Not a puzzle to solve. In the New Testament a mystery is something hidden for ages and now spoken aloud. And the secret God kept and then revealed is this: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.

**The mystery is a people, not a doctrine**

We might have expected the great revealed mystery to be a teaching, a fact about God's inner life. It is, instead, a people. The thing hidden for ages was that the far-off nations would be brought into one body on equal terms. The mystery is the church — Jew and Gentile in a single fellowship, fellow heirs of the same inheritance.

And then Paul says something that should reframe how we think about every congregation. "So that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 3:10). Through the church. The audience is not even mainly human; it is the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places, the same powers Paul will arm us against in chapter six. God's plan is to put his wisdom on display before the watching cosmos, and the exhibit he has chosen is the church.

That means the ordinary, frustrating, mixed congregation you belong to is not a holding pen until heaven. It is the demonstration. When people who would never otherwise share a table share one body, the universe is being shown the wisdom of God. I have sat in elders' meetings small and slow and wondered what eternal weight any of it carried. This is the answer. Heaven is watching the church learn to be one.

**The prayer that bows**

In verse fourteen Paul finally returns to the sentence he abandoned, and it comes back as a prayer. "For this reason I bow my knees before the Father." He does not pray that they would have more. He prays for power — "that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being." Power, in Paul's prayer, is not for spectacle. It is the strength to grasp something.

To grasp what? "That you, being rooted and grounded in love, may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge." He prays for power to know a love that exceeds knowing. It takes strength because the love of Christ is larger than the mind that reaches for it, and we are forever tempted to settle for a love we can measure and manage.

I confess I want a love I can fit in my hands, a love proportioned to my obedience. Paul prays me out of that. He asks God to make me strong enough to be overwhelmed.

**Filled to the fullness of God**

The prayer ends impossibly: "that you may be filled with all the fullness of God." A finite vessel filled with an infinite God. It cannot be done, and Paul knows it, which is why he closes with the doxology: "Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations."

Glory in the church. The Christ connection runs straight through: the church exists because Christ gathered the far-off into his one body, and through that body God shows the powers his wisdom. The congregation is not the means to the display. The congregation is the display.

The church is God's wisdom on display.

There is a hinge in this letter, and it turns on a single word: therefore. For three chapters Paul has described what God has done — chosen, redeemed, raised, gathered. Now he says, "I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called" (Ephesians 4:1). Everything before the hinge is gift. Everything after is the life that fits the gift. He does not say walk worthy in order to be called. He says you have been called; now walk worthy of it.

And the first mark of a worthy walk is not zeal or eloquence. It is the willingness to bear with people who are hard to bear with.

**Keep the unity you were given**

"With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Read what Paul asks and what he does not. He does not ask us to create unity. He asks us to maintain it, to keep it. The unity already exists, made by the Spirit at the cross, and our job is to guard it, not to manufacture it.

Then he grounds it in seven ones. One body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Our unity is not an achievement of agreeable personalities. It rests on the oneness of God himself. To fracture the church is not merely to fall out with a brother; it is to contradict the one God who made us one body.

I have to name how easily I excuse my own contributions to division. I dress impatience as discernment and call my factions conviction. Paul gives no room for it. The bond of peace is kept by humility, gentleness, patience, and bearing with one another — four words that describe not the strong personality but the crucified one.

**The ascended Christ gives gifts**

Unity does not mean sameness. "But grace was given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ's gift." The risen and ascended Christ — the one who descended and then ascended far above all the heavens that he might fill all things — distributes gifts to his body. And the gifts Paul names here are people: apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers.

Notice why they are given. "To equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ." The gifted leaders are not given to do the ministry while the saints watch. They are given to equip the saints so that the saints do the ministry. A church where the work belongs to the staff and the pews receive a performance has misread this verse. The pastor's task is to work himself outward, to hand the ministry to the body. I take that as a rebuke of every instinct in me to keep the work in my own hands because it is faster, or because it flatters me to be needed.

**Grow up into the head**

The goal is maturity. "Until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ." Children, Paul says, are tossed around by every wind of doctrine and human cunning. The mark of a grown-up church is that it can no longer be blown over by the latest clever thing.

And the way it grows is by "speaking the truth in love" so that "we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ, from whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love."

There is the Christ connection, and it is structural. He is the head. The body grows only as it grows into him, drawing from him, held together by him. We do not build the church into unity by our programs. We grow into a unity Christ already secured, each part working, the whole body building itself up in love.

Unity is kept, not built.

Anyone who has lost a great deal of weight knows the strange afterlife of the old clothes. They still hang in the closet. They still fit the memory of who you were. And there is a temptation, on a low day, to put them back on, because the old shape is familiar even when it no longer fits. Paul writes to people who have been changed and are still tempted to wear the old life because it is familiar.

He begins bluntly. "Now this I say and testify in the Lord, that you must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds" (Ephesians 4:17). You must no longer. The old walk is not an option still on the table. Something has happened that makes returning to it a contradiction.

**Put off, put on**

The logic is clothing. "To put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires, and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness." Put off, put on. The old self is taken off like a garment that belongs to a person you no longer are. The new self is put on, and it is created after the likeness of God — not self-improved, created.

But Paul does not stay abstract. He gets specific in a way that is almost uncomfortable. Stop lying; speak truth to your neighbor. Be angry, but do not let the sun go down on your anger. Let the thief no longer steal but work and give. Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only what builds up. Put away bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, slander. Be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.

That last clause is the engine of the whole section. We forgive as God in Christ forgave us. The new self does not run on willpower; it runs on having been forgiven at the cross and then handing that same forgiveness outward.

**Walk in love, walk in light**

Then Paul lifts the standard impossibly high. "Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God." The measure of our love is not affection but self-giving — the Christ who gave himself up. That is what we put on.

And he changes the image from clothing to light. "For at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light." Notice he does not say you were in darkness. You were darkness. Now you are light. The change is not your surroundings; it is your identity. The deeds of darkness are to be exposed, because anything exposed by light becomes visible, and what becomes visible can no longer pretend.

I will not preach this from above it. I know the deceitful desires Paul names. I know the corrupting talk that builds nothing, the bitterness I have nursed past sundown and called principle. This passage does not flatter me. It strips me and asks why I keep the old coat in the closet at all.

**Filled, not numbed**

The section ends with a contrast that cuts to the heart of it. "And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit." The old life reaches for what numbs and inflames. The new life is filled with the Spirit — and the evidence Paul gives is not ecstasy but ordinary worship and gratitude: addressing one another in psalms and hymns, singing, giving thanks always, submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.

There is the Christ connection again, all the way through: forgive as God in Christ forgave, love as Christ loved and gave himself. The new self is not a better version of the old one. It is a self created after God, clothed in the love of the Christ who gave himself away. Take off the old coat. It does not fit you anymore.

You are not who you were.

I have officiated weddings where the room went quiet at a certain word, and not the word people expect. Not submit. The word that stops the room, when it is read honestly, is the word to the husbands. Because the standard set for him is a cross.

Paul moves the great themes of this letter — the one body, the love of Christ, the dwelling of God — straight into the household. Having said "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ," he then addresses the home one member at a time. And what governs the whole passage is a comparison he could not have made larger.

**The husband under the cross**

Wives are told to submit to their husbands as to the Lord. That command is real, and Paul means it. But watch where the weight falls. Three verses to the wife, nine to the husband, and the standard he sets crushes any notion that this passage props up male comfort. "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25). As Christ loved the church and gave himself up. The model for a husband's authority is a man dying for the people in his care.

This is not headship as privilege. It is headship as sacrifice. The husband who reads this looking for his rights has not read it. Christ's love for the church was expenditure — he gave himself up to make her holy. A man who loves like that has no energy left for lording it over anyone. I have to say plainly that I have failed my own household far more often by neglect than by tyranny, and this text indicts the quiet man who withholds himself just as surely as the harsh one. To love as Christ loved is to spend yourself, and most of us would rather keep ourselves.

**The mystery underneath the marriage**

Then Paul reveals what the whole arrangement has been pointing at. Quoting Genesis — the two shall become one flesh — he says, "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church." Marriage was never finally about marriage. It was a sign, from the beginning, of Christ and his bride. Every faithful husband, every responsive wife, has been a living picture of a larger marriage between the Lord and his people.

That raises the stakes on the ordinary home past anything sentiment can carry. When a husband gives himself up and a wife responds in trust, they are not merely getting along. They are displaying the gospel at the kitchen table. The same church that displays God's wisdom to the powers in chapter three displays the love of Christ in the marriages of its members.

**Children, fathers, servants, masters**

Paul keeps going down through the household. Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right — and he attaches the first commandment with a promise. Then, immediately, a word that would have startled the ancient world: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord." The father with all the power is told to restrain it, to consider the child's heart, not to exasperate. As a father of sons I read that and feel it land. The temptation of strength is to use it carelessly, and the gospel forbids it in the home first.

Then servants and masters, and Paul levels the ground between them with a single sentence: "knowing that whatever good anyone does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is a slave or free." And to masters: do the same to them, "and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him." The man with earthly authority is reminded he has a Master too, who does not weigh him by his rank.

The Christ connection is the spine of all of it. The marriage points to Christ and the church. The father's restraint imitates the Father. The master answers to the Master in heaven. The gospel does not stop at the church door; it walks home and reorders the table.

The gospel reaches the kitchen table.

Soldiers who have been in combat will tell you that the hardest thing is not the charge. It is holding the line. Anyone can be brave in a forward rush. To stand, hour after hour, when the ground is contested and you are tired and the enemy is patient — that is what breaks men. Paul ends this letter not with a call to advance but with a call to stand, and he says it four times.

"Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil" (Ephesians 6:10-11). Be strong in the Lord. Not in yourself. The first word of the whole battle plan is that the strength is borrowed.

**The enemy you cannot see**

Paul names the conflict with precision. "For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places." Not flesh and blood. The people across the table, the family member who wounded you, the colleague you have decided is the problem — they are not the war. Behind the visible conflict stands an unseen one, and the church that spends itself fighting flesh and blood is fighting the wrong enemy with the wrong weapons.

This matters pastorally more than we admit. I have watched believers exhaust themselves in bitterness against a person, never once suspecting there was a power behind the trouble that wanted exactly that bitterness. Paul lifts our eyes. The schemes are real, the powers are real, and they are stronger than we are. Which is why the armor is not ours.

**The armor is God's**

Every piece Paul lists belongs to God before it belongs to us. The belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shoes of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith with which to extinguish the flaming darts, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit which is the word of God. Read the Old Testament behind it and you find that righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet are first described as the armor of God himself. We are not issued private gear. We are clothed in his.

So the command, repeated, is to stand. "Take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm." Having done all, to stand. The aim is not a glorious advance that overruns the enemy by our strength. It is to be found still standing when the smoke clears, held up by armor that was never our own.

I confess I prefer the language of victory to the language of standing. Standing sounds passive, unimpressive. But Paul knows what he is asking. To still be there, still believing, still unmoved after the evil day has done its worst, is not small. It is the whole point.

**Praying at all times**

And then the armor passage ends not with a weapon but with prayer. "Praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints." The soldier's posture is a man on his knees, alert, praying for the others on the line. Paul even asks them to pray for him, a prisoner, that words would be given him to speak the gospel boldly. The great apostle does not stand alone. He needs the supplication of the saints.

The Christ connection holds the whole thing together. Be strong in the Lord. The strength of his might, the same might that raised Christ and seated him over every ruler and authority named in this letter, is the strength in which we stand. The powers we face have already been put under his feet. We are not fighting toward a victory in doubt. We are holding ground that Christ already won, in armor that is his, by strength that is his.

Stand. The strength is his.
